title: Body and health
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE BODY PART IS THE SUBJECT, and that is the whole delta. bolít and bolyát are L2-M8's rows and nothing about them changes here — what changes is that the verb agrees with the part that hurts: u menyá bolít golová, one head, but u menyá bolyát zúby, several teeth. You are not in the sentence as a subject at all; u menyá names the owner, exactly as it names the owner of a car in L1-M4.

English puts the sufferer first — "I have a headache", "my throat hurts" — and Russian puts the part first and the person in a corner. There is no word for "my" in any of these sentences: moyá golová bolít is grammatical and sounds like a medical report about a head. The everyday sentence is u menyá bolít golová, and a learner who reaches for moy here will do it for years.

k + DATIVE is how Russian goes to a PERSON, where v and na go to a place: ya idú k vrachú but ya idú v aptéku. L2-M4 opened the accusative of motion for places and left people unnamed; this is the seat it left empty. The case itself is L2-M1's dative doing ordinary work, so what is new is one preposition and not a new set of endings.

A symptom is something you HAVE, and the sentence has no verb in it: u menyá temperatúra, u menyá káshel', u menyá násmork. This is L1-M4's possession frame — u plus the genitive of the owner — doing health, so the whole shape is already yours and the only spend is the vocabulary. Add yest' only when the point is that the thing exists at all.

Duration takes the ACCUSATIVE with no preposition — bolít uzhé dva dnya — where English needs "for". uzhé ("already") is what carries the still-true reading, because Russian has no perfect tense whatsoever: bolít is a plain present, and "it has been hurting for two days" is that present plus one adverb. Nothing here is a new tense, and there is no new tense coming.

words.note: Throat — and here it is the SUBJECT of L2-M8's bolít. The part does the hurting; you are only its owner, named by u menyá at the front.

sentences.trap: No moyó anywhere. u menyá already says whose throat it is, and adding a possessive makes it sound like a case file.
sentences.sound: u mi-NYA ba-LIT GOR-la. górlo is stressed on the first syllable, unlike almost everything else in this module.

mistake.why: ya cannot stand there: the throat is the subject and the verb agrees with it. The person goes into u menyá.

sentences.usage: The first line of any visit to a doctor.
sentences.mnemonic: At me — hurts — throat. The part comes last and does the work.

words.note: Teeth, plural — so L2-M8's bolít becomes bolyát, agreeing with them and not with you. One tooth on its own is zub, and then the verb goes back to bolít.

sentences.trap: bolyát is not a new verb, it is the plural of the one L2-M8 taught. The number of the body part decides which you say.
sentences.sound: u mi-NYA ba-LYAT ZU-by. bolít and bolyát differ only in that last vowel, and it carries the whole plural.

variations.changed: one tooth, so the verb goes singular

mistake.why: Teeth are plural and the verb has to follow them: bolyát. The mistake is invisible in English, where "hurt" looks the same either way.

sentences.usage: Ringing a dentist, which is the sentence this module is really for.
sentences.mnemonic: One zub bolít, many zúby bolyát.

sentences.display: U menyá bolít golová uzhé dva dnya
sentences.script: У меня болит голова уже два дня
sentences.cue: I've had a headache for two days
sentences.literal: At me hurts head already two of-day

words.note: The counted shape of den'. A stretch of time is bare — dva dnya, no preposition where English says "for". M8 gives this counting its rule; here it is one phrase to keep.

sentences.trap: There is no "have been" to build. bolít is an ordinary present, and uzhé is the whole of the English perfect.
sentences.sound: u mi-NYA ba-LIT ga-la-VA u-ZHE dva DNYA. dnya is one syllable and takes the fall of the line.

variations.cue: It's been hurting for two days
variations.changed: the part left out, as in speech

variations.display: U neyó bolít golová uzhé dva dnya
variations.script: У неё болит голова уже два дня
variations.cue: She's had a headache for two days

mistake.display: U menyá bolít golová za dva dnya
mistake.script: У меня болит голова за два дня
mistake.why: za is not "for" in this sense. Duration takes the bare accusative and nothing in front of it: uzhé dva dnya.

sentences.usage: Explaining that this is not new, which is what a doctor asks next.
sentences.mnemonic: uzhé plus a plain present — no perfect required.

words.note: "To" for PEOPLE, and it takes the dative. Places keep v and na: k vrachú but v aptéku. Before some clusters it is said ko — ko mne, to my place.
The dative of L2-M8's vrach — see that row for the word itself. Only the case is new here, and it is L2-M1's dative doing ordinary work.

sentences.trap: v vrachá is not a sentence. A person is never a destination with v: people take k plus the dative.
sentences.sound: ya i-DU k vra-CHU. The k has no vowel of its own and leans onto the word after it.

variations.cue: I need to see a doctor
variations.changed: L2-M1's nádo, with the verb left out

mistake.why: v is for places. To a person it is k plus the dative: k vrachú.

sentences.usage: Saying where you are off to, at work or at home.
sentences.mnemonic: k for people, v for places.

words.note: A fever is something you HAVE, and the sentence needs no verb: u menyá temperatúra. In Russian the word alone already means a raised one.

sentences.trap: No yest' here. u menyá yest' answers whether the thing exists at all; a symptom is simply reported.
sentences.sound: u mi-NYA tim-pi-ra-TU-ra. One stress, on the TU — the first three syllables run together.

variations.changed: the past, agreeing with the symptom

mistake.why: The verb "to have" exists but almost nobody uses it of themselves. Health lives in u menyá.

sentences.usage: The line that keeps you at home for the day.
sentences.mnemonic: At me — a temperature. No verb needed.

sentences.cue: I have a cough and a runny nose

words.note: A cough, and the stress is on the first syllable: KA-shel'. Like every symptom here it is simply had, not done — u menyá káshel'.

words.cue: a runny nose, a head cold
words.note: The blocked, running nose of an ordinary cold — one word where English needs three. Stress on the first syllable: NAS-mork.

sentences.trap: Both are singular nouns and neither takes an article or a verb. Two symptoms simply sit side by side with i.
sentences.sound: u mi-NYA KA-shil i NAS-mark. Both words are front-heavy; the endings fall away to a soft a.

variations.display: U menyá káshel' uzhé dva dnya
variations.script: У меня кашель уже два дня
variations.cue: I've had a cough for two days
variations.changed: how long it has gone on

mistake.why: That says you ARE a cough. The frame is u menyá plus the symptom, and it never takes ya.

sentences.usage: The chemist's counter, and the message to your colleague.
sentences.mnemonic: KA-shel' and NAS-mork — both hit at the front.

words.note: A place, so it keeps L2-M4's motion frame: v plus the accusative, aptéku. Standing in it is v aptéke, and the shop itself is aptéka.

sentences.trap: Set this against S04. Same verb, same trip, but a place takes v and a person takes k.
sentences.sound: ya i-DU v ap-TYE-ku. The v is a single consonant glued to the front of aptéku.

variations.display: Ya idú v aptéku, potóm domóy
variations.script: Я иду в аптеку, потом домой
variations.cue: I'm going to the chemist's, then home

mistake.why: k would mean you are heading towards the building to stand outside it. Going in is v aptéku.

sentences.usage: Everyday errands, said on the way out of the door.
sentences.mnemonic: k vrachú, v aptéku — the person and the place.

sentences.display: U menyá bolyát rúki i nógi
sentences.script: У меня болят руки и ноги
sentences.literal: At me hurt arms and legs

words.note: One word for the whole limb, hand and arm together; nogá does the same for leg and foot. Plural subject, so the verb is bolyát again.

sentences.trap: Russian does not split hand from arm or foot from leg. Which one is meant is left to the situation.
sentences.sound: u mi-NYA ba-LYAT RU-ki i NO-gi. Both nouns move their stress to the front in the plural.

mistake.why: u menyá has already said they are yours. moí on top of it is one possessive too many.

sentences.usage: The end of a day of carrying things.
sentences.mnemonic: ruká alone, rúki together — and the stress jumps forward.

words.note: Back, stressed on the ending like golová and ruká — the three commonest complaints in the language all stress their last syllable.
The belly, not the organ: u menyá bolít zhivót is what a child says and what an adult says. Stress on the ending, as with spiná.

sentences.trap: Still no possessive and still no ya. Every one of these sentences is built the same way.
sentences.sound: u mi-NYA ba-LIT spi-NA. Four of the five syllables are unstressed and short.

mistake.why: Grammatical, and it sounds like a line from a report. People say u menyá bolít spiná.

sentences.usage: What you tell a physiotherapist, and everyone else.
sentences.mnemonic: golová, ruká, spiná — the aches all stress the end.

sentences.display: Ya výpil tablétku, i mne stálo lúchshe
sentences.script: Я выпил таблетку, и мне стало лучше
sentences.cue: I took a tablet and felt better
sentences.literal: I drank tablet, and to-me became better

words.note: Accusative after výpit' — Russians DRINK a tablet where English takes one. The plain form is tablétka and two or more are tablétki.

sentences.trap: "I have taken a tablet" has no separate form here. výpil is the only past there is, and it already means the job is done.
sentences.sound: ya VY-pil tab-LYET-ku, i mnye STA-la LUCH-she. A short pause at the comma before i.

variations.display: Oná výpila tablétku i poshlá na rabótu
variations.script: Она выпила таблетку и пошла на работу
variations.cue: She took a tablet and went to work
variations.changed: two finished steps in a row

mistake.display: Ya vzyal tablétku i mne stálo lúchshe
mistake.script: Я взял таблетку и мне стало лучше
mistake.why: vzyal is taking it in your hand. Swallowing it is výpil, the same verb as drinking.

sentences.usage: Reporting that something worked, in one line.
sentences.mnemonic: You drink a tablet in Russian.
